newsitem.title: GHANA: Close race in Ghana poll, monitors satisfied.
newsitem.headline: Close race in Ghana poll, monitors satisfied.

text.p: Ghana's populist president Jerry Rawlings looked to have a fight on his hands on Sunday with his main rival John Kufuor and his opposition alliance edging into an early lead after presidential and parliamentary elections.
Provisional results from Saturday's elections showed that with about 6.5 percent of constituencies declared, Kufuor had 259,230 votes compared to 199,373 for Rawlings.

In the contest for parliament's 200 seats, which was being tallied separately, the alliance of Kufuor's New Patriotic Party and the People's Convention Party had won nine seats compared to eight for Rawlings's National Democratic Congress.
The Commonwealth Observer Group, among around 100 foreign observers monitoring the poll, paid tribute to the organisation and conduct of the election.
"We believe that the conditions existed for a free expression of will by the electors," the 23-member mission said in a statement on Sunday.
Political pundits predicted a neck-and-neck race for the West African gold and cocoa producer's presidency, which Rawlings was hoping to win for a final four-year term.

Rawlings, who is half-Scottish and still only 49, has been called everything from a dictator to a messiah. He twice seized power in the former British colony, first in 1979, when he executed three former heads of state, and then in 1981.

A former socialist firebrand, he converted to Western-style free-market economics -- winning plaudits from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. He made the transition to elected president in disputed 1992 elections.
A key question was whether his crowd-pulling populism would bring him victory in the face of widespread unemployment and high inflation which have fuelled popular discontent.
"As at now, returns are coming in from the strong areas of Kufuor," a senior official from Rawlings's party told Reuters, predicting an outright majority for the president.

The main opposition, campaigning under the banner of the Great Alliance, learned the lesson of going into the 1992 multi-party elections in disarray and, against the odds, formed a common front for this year's elections.
Kufuor, a seasoned politician and a businessman who was celebrating his 58th birthday on Sunday, took the medium-sized provincial towns of Cape Coast, Sekondi, Sunyani, Koforidua and part of Tamale.

Early results from the national election commission showed Employment and Social Welfare Minister David Sarpong Boateng losing his seat in parliament as did the government chief whip and a couple of regional ministers.
Unofficial returns from a handful of polling stations in the capital Accra showed Rawlings taking a lead in more populous poorer areas with Kufuor edging ahead in wealthier districts.
One result in Kufuor's stronghold in Kumasi, Ghana's second city and capital of the mighty pre-colonial Ashanti empire, suggested that he could look forward to a landslide there.

Ghanaians voted peacefully and in large numbers. National Election Commission chairman Kwadwo Afari-Gyan told Reuters on Sunday that the estimated turnout was 70 percent. More than nine million of Ghana's 17.5 million people were eligible to vote.

Pundits gave little chance to the third contender, surgeon Edward Mahama of the People's National Convention, but his presence could force a run-off, which must be held within 21 days in the event of no outright winner.
